scope:
Reviewed: agent loop (src/agent.py), MCP client (src/mcp_client.py), policy enforcement (src/policy.py), budgets (src/budgets.py), container/K8s configuration (Dockerfile, k8s/deployment.yaml, k8s/networkpolicy.yaml), credentials and revocation (src/auth.py, src/killswitch.py), audit logging (src/audit.py), tools (src/tools/), configuration (config/agent.yaml), system prompt (prompts/system.md), .mcp.json, CODEOWNERS. Not reviewed: database schema, CI/CD deployment pipeline (not present in repo), runtime behavior, upstream services (Zendesk, Stripe, Gmail, Qdrant), cluster-level policies beyond the namespace. Reviewed config/agent.yaml, .mcp.json, k8s/deployment.yaml, Dockerfile, requirements.txt, CODEOWNERS, src/agent.py, src/telemetry.py, src/agent_type_id.py, src/audit.py, src/policy.py, src/budgets.py, README.md, and prompts/system.md. No CI/CD workflows, test suites, or rollback procedures found in the repo. No dedicated release manifest file or recovery procedure. Model configuration uses a changeable alias rather than a pinned version. Reviewed: .mcp.json MCP server config, src/main.py webhook handler, src/agent.py main loop, 
src/auth.py credential handling, src/policy.py policy checks, src/audit.py audit logging, 
src/killswitch.py shutdown mechanism, src/mcp_client.py tool loading, src/tools/ local tools,
config/agent.yaml agent config, k8s/deployment.yaml and networkpolicy.yaml, 
Dockerfile, requirements.txt, README.md, prompts/system.md.

Not reviewed: External services (Zendesk, Stripe, Gmail, Qdrant) implementation, 
deployment-time secrets management, network infrastructure outside the agent manifest,
B/R/A/C aspects (different review passes). Reviewed: agent loop in src/agent.py, tool implementations in src/tools/, input validation in src/main.py, kill switch in src/killswitch.py, audit logging in src/audit.py, telemetry in src/telemetry.py, retrieval in src/retrieval.py, policy in src/policy.py, Kubernetes deployment in k8s/, configuration in config/. Not reviewed: tests (not included), external SIEM/detection rules, production deployment of Redis/Qdrant, end-to-end injection testing.

findings.title: Minimal tool surface

evidence.note: anthropic_tools() returns all MCP tools with no filtering
stripe MCP configured with '--tools=all' wildcard
tools list combines local schemas plus all MCP tools

checks.check: Each agent role has one explicit allowlist of tool names, with no wildcard grants such as `*`, `mcp__*`, `Bash(*)`, or `bypassPermissions`.
checks.note: No explicit allowlist found in code or config; policy.py has only a blocklist

checks.check: Tools discovered from MCP servers are filtered against that allowlist before the model can see or call them.
checks.note: All tools from MCP servers are added without checking an allowlist

checks.check: The dispatcher rejects a call to any tool name not on the allowlist, instead of looking it up dynamically.
checks.note: Dispatcher assumes any tool name in LOCAL_TOOLS or MCP tool_index is valid; no rejection of unlisted names

checks.check: Allow and approval decisions never read server-supplied hints or descriptions such as `readOnlyHint` or 'read-only'.
checks.note: Policy check only uses tool name and arguments, not server-supplied hints

checks.check: File access is limited to named directories, not the whole filesystem.
checks.note: Local tools use database queries and HTTP calls; no direct file access visible in agent code

red_flags_found: src/mcp_client.py:36-50 anthropic_tools() accepts every tool from MCP servers with no allowlist filter
.mcp.json:12 Stripe configured with '--tools=all' to use all available tools
findings.summary: Agent has no explicit allowlist of tools; MCP servers provide all tools without filtering.
findings.next_step: Define an explicit allowlist of approved tool names in config; filter MCP tool list before passing to model; update dispatcher to reject unlisted tools.

findings.title: Least-privilege access

evidence.note: resolve_user_token reuses support rep's OAuth token
MCP servers receive OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN from user_token
Support rep's Authorization header passed to run_ticket

checks.check: The agent's IAM policy or role names specific actions and resources, with no `*` action or resource and no owner, editor, or cluster-admin role.
checks.note: No IAM policy visible in this repo; need to check cloud platform (AWS/GCP/Azure) permissions

checks.check: Tenant scope is enforced in the credential or the data layer (token claim, row-level security, or per-tenant account), not by the prompt or by code the model's output controls.
checks.quote: "SELECT stripe_payment_intent, total_cents FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = %s AND order_number = %s",
checks.note: [fix: was yes; has a quote that isn't in the cited file near the cited line] Tools enforce tenant scope in database queries; tenant_id is passed as parameter and checked in WHERE clause

checks.check: Tokens are issued with a set audience, and receiving services reject tokens whose audience does not match.
checks.note: Unclear if OAuth tokens have audience claims or if downstream services check them

checks.check: The agent uses its own service identity, not a human user's token, a copied session, or an admin key.
checks.quote:
def resolve_user_token(authorization_header: str) -> UserToken:
    """Reuse the support rep's OAuth access token for downstream calls."
checks.note: Agent explicitly reuses the support rep's user token instead of using a service account

red_flags_found: src/auth.py:12-21 Agent uses support rep's OAuth token for all downstream calls (Zendesk, Stripe, Gmail)
findings.summary: Agent reuses support rep's OAuth token instead of using its own service identity.
findings.next_step: Create a service account for the agent with specific scopes for Zendesk, Stripe, and Gmail; configure each MCP server with agent credentials, not user credentials; update auth.py to use agent identity.

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and other secrets from Kubernetes Secret

checks.note: INTERNAL_API_KEY from environment variable is placed into system prompt template

checks.check: Where the service supports it, tokens are bound to their holder with mTLS, DPoP, or workload proof tokens.
checks.note: Unclear if tokens have mTLS, DPoP, or workload proofs; would require cloud platform audit

prompts/system.md:11 Prompt template includes placeholder for internal_api_key

findings.title: Independent revocation

evidence.note: Halt flag checked before each model call
Agent uses user's token so user revocation blocks agent

checks.check: A revocation control disables the agent's own identity or credentials without disabling the user who launched it.
checks.note: Operator halt flag exists but agent identity is fundamentally tied to support rep's OAuth token; revoking the user disables the agent, so they're not independent

checks.check: Revocation is applied at a trusted enforcement point (identity provider, gateway, or target service) and does not need the agent's cooperation.
checks.note: Killswitch is a trusted enforcement point, but agent identity is reused from user token; revocation of user token needs cooperation from upstream OAuth provider, not just the agent's killswitch

checks.check: Later calls are blocked even with cached tokens, self-contained tokens, and open sessions: token lifetime is shorter than the revocation limit, or revocation is pushed to each service (for example CAEP) or checked on every call.
checks.note: Agent uses long-lived OAuth tokens passed through headers; if token is cached or session is open, revocation may not block it immediately

checks.check: Revocation covers access tokens and open sessions, not only the refresh token.
checks.note: Halt covers the agent's access token in one layer, but user token can be long-lived and other services may have open sessions; revocation isn't pushed to downstream services

red_flags_found: src/auth.py:12-21 Agent identity is tied to support rep's OAuth token; revoking user cuts off agent
src/killswitch.py: Halt flag provides operator control but not independent of user credential
findings.summary: Killswitch blocks agent but revocation tied to user token lifecycle.
findings.next_step: Create separate service identity for agent; implement token revocation push (e.g., CAEP) to downstream services; establish and test revocation SLA.

findings.title: Destructive-action interception

evidence.note: BLOCKED_TOOLS blocklist used instead of allowlist
policy.allowed() checks only tool name, not arguments
Prompt says 'refunds under $500 do not need manager' but no enforcement

checks.check: High-impact operations are listed in code or config and blocked by default, including deletes, destructive updates, force-pushes, infrastructure teardown, payment changes, outbound sends, and deleting audit records or changing their retention.
checks.note: Only 4 tools blocked by name; many other destructive operations possible (e.g., issue_refund, stripe refunds, delete messages)

checks.check: The gate runs in the execution path when the call runs and checks the operation, the target, and the arguments, not only a tool name, command name, or blocklist of words.
checks.note: policy.allowed() checks only tool name; arguments are passed but not checked by policy

checks.check: The same gate covers every path that can do the operation, including raw shell, HTTP or API clients, other tools, and requests to a more powerful tool or peer agent.
checks.quote:
def allowed(tool_name: str, arguments: dict) -> bool:
    return tool_name not in BLOCKED_TOOLS
checks.note: No coverage of shell, SQL, or raw HTTP paths; MCP servers may provide raw API tools (e.g., stripe refunds_create)

checks.check: A blocked operation runs only after approval from a person or system with higher authority than the agent; a prompt, comment, or model instruction is never the enforcement.
checks.quote: If an order arrived damaged or late, refund it. Refunds under $500 do not need a manager.
checks.note: Approval limit stated in prompt only; not enforced in code; no approval workflow for high-impact actions

checks.check: For an agent that reads untrusted input, reaches sensitive data or systems, and acts outside, every consequential action is gated, unless code shows untrusted content cannot pick the tool, destination, or arguments (for example plan-then-execute or capability tracking).
checks.quote: The agent: reads untrusted input (Zendesk ticket), reaches sensitive data (orders, payments), acts outside (Stripe refunds, email)
checks.note: Agent combines all three capabilities; only some actions are nominally blocked, but no approval enforcement; untrusted content (ticket body) goes straight to model

red_flags_found: src/policy.py:11-12 Blocklist approach: tool_name not in BLOCKED_TOOLS is insufficient; allows all unlisted destructive tools
src/agent.py:92 policy.allowed() checks tool name only, not operation semantics or arguments
prompts/system.md:6 Refund approval limit ($500) stated in prompt but not enforced in code
src/mcp_client.py:40-50 Stripe MCP provides raw stripe API tools (like 'refunds_create') without gating
findings.summary: Destructive actions guarded only by blocklist; no approval gate; policy checks tool name, not arguments.
findings.next_step: List all high-impact operations and their parameters; add approval gate in execution path; check operation, target, and arguments; require explicit approval for refunds, deletes, etc.

findings.title: Approval integrity

evidence.note: Policy is blocklist-only, no approval flow

checks.check: Each approval record is bound to the requesting agent instance and to the exact operation, target, arguments, and scope, and records the approver and an expiry time.
checks.note: No approval record structure found in code

checks.check: When the action runs, the gate rejects it if the instance, operation, target, or arguments differ from the approval, or if the approval has expired.
checks.note: No approval checking at execution time

checks.check: Each use of an approval is recorded in one atomic step (single-use or a bounded counter), so replays and parallel calls cannot go past the grant.
checks.note: No approval consumption tracking

checks.check: The gate checks that the approver has authority for this action, and rechecks permissions and the relevant resource state when the action runs.
checks.note: No approver authority check or resource state recheck

checks.check: If the approval service errors or cannot be reached, the action is denied.
checks.note: No approval service; no fail-closed handling

red_flags_found: No approval service or workflow found in codebase
High-impact actions (refunds, deletes) have no approval gate
findings.summary: No approval mechanism exists for high-impact actions.
findings.next_step: Build approval service with atomically consumed approvals; tie each approval to specific operation, target, arguments, and agent instance; implement recheck of permissions and resource state at execution time.

findings.title: Hard execution budgets

evidence.note: RunBudget class enforces limits outside model
Budget limits configured with specific values
Budget checked on each step and tool call

checks.check: Limits on loop count, run time, tokens, cost, tool-call rate, and number of sub-agents started are set in code or config.
checks.quote:
budgets:
  max_steps: 12
  max_wall_seconds: 120
  max_total_tokens: 60000
  max_tool_calls_per_minute: 30
  tenant_daily_cost_usd: 40.0
  fleet_daily_cost_usd: 1500.0
checks.note: Limits set for loop steps, wall-clock time, tokens, tool-call rate, and daily spend per tenant and fleet

checks.check: The harness or a gateway outside the model enforces each limit and stops or escalates the run when it is hit; the model cannot raise, reset, or skip them.
checks.note: Harness checks budgets and raises BudgetExceeded outside model; model cannot raise or reset limits

checks.check: Budgets apply to nested sub-agents, so their usage counts against the limits.
checks.note: No nested sub-agent spawning visible in code; can't confirm if budgets apply to sub-agents because none exist in this agent

checks.check: Spend and rate quotas also apply per user or service, per tenant, and across the fleet, counted across runs, not only within one run.
checks.quote:
class TenantQuota:
    """Daily spend caps per tenant and across the whole fleet, shared through Redis."""
checks.note: TenantQuota enforces both tenant_daily_cost_usd and fleet_daily_cost_usd across all runs

findings.summary: Run budgets enforced outside model; per-tenant and fleet quotas tracked in Redis.
findings.next_step: Verify budgets are tested in production-like conditions; confirm quota enforcement persists across rolling restarts.

findings.title: Environment isolation

evidence.note: Egress rule allows all traffic

checks.check: Network policy or security groups default-deny and allow only the listed systems and data stores the agent needs.
checks.note: Egress rule is empty dict, which allows all traffic; should default-deny with explicit allow list

checks.check: No route, mount, or credential gives the runtime a path to unapproved production resources, admin systems, host services, or other tenants. Egress to 0.0.0.0/0 or another broad range, even only on ports 80 and 443, is such a route: it reaches cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) and internal services unless they are explicitly blocked.
checks.note: No network policy preventing access to unapproved systems; egress to 0.0.0.0/0 is allowed which includes metadata and internal services

checks.check: Isolation is enforced in infrastructure config, not by the prompt or by agent code the model can influence.
checks.note: Isolation is defined in infrastructure (NetworkPolicy), not in prompt or agent code

red_flags_found: k8s/networkpolicy.yaml:18-19 Egress rule is [{}] which means allow all; violates default-deny principle
findings.summary: NetworkPolicy allows all egress; agent can reach any external host.
findings.next_step: Replace egress: [{}] with default-deny and allow only specific destinations (Zendesk, Stripe, Gmail, Qdrant, OTLP); test that blocked destinations fail.
